sections.html:
• Name: Dwarf puffer fish
  • Other names: Malabar Puffer Fish, Dwarf Pea Puffer, Pea Puffer Fish, Pygmy Pufferfish, Dwarf Pufferfish
  • Water type: Freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres (5 gallons)
  • Size: up to 2–2.5 cm (0.8–1 inch)
  • Optimal temperature: 24–27°C (75–80°F)
  • Optimal pH: 7.0–8.0
  • Optimal GH: 7–14
  • Dwellers: mid and bottom-dwelling
  • Nitrate: less than 60
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Life span: up to 6 years
  • Colour: yellowish and whitish with dark patches
  • Keeping: medium; breeding: medium-difficult

Carinotetraodon travancoricus is one of the smallest puffer fishes in the world. Despite its miniature size and "puppy" eyes, it is predatory and best kept in a tropical, species-only aquarium, as it can be quite aggressive and territorial.

In India, Carinotetraodon travancoricus has been exploited extensively for the aquarium trade. As a result, it was listed as vulnerable by the IUCN in 2010. Fortunately, this species is now successfully bred in captivity and available for sale.

Dwarf puffer fish are a little more high maintenance than other fish, and keeping them in a community tank is not easy.

Carinotetraodon travancoricus is endemic to rivers of the Western Ghats in South India.

It is mainly distributed in the Chalakkudy, Pamba, Periyar, Kabani, Bharathapuzha, Vamanapuram and Muvattupuzha rivers, Lake Vembanad and the kole wetlands of Thrissur, Kallar stream and Neyyar wildlife sanctuary of south Kerala.

The inferred extent of occurrence is around 35,000 to 36,000 km².

Carinotetraodon travancoricus inhabits heavily vegetated, slow-moving fresh waters. Its natural environment is composed of mud and sand. In the wild, Dwarf puffer fish dominate in areas with gathered Cabomba plants, which provide essential habitat and food.

The minimum tank size for a single Dwarf puffer fish is generally considered to be 20 litres (5 gallons).

For a small group (3–4 fish), a tank of at least 40 litres (10 gallons) is a good starting point. A larger tank is always recommended to accommodate their territorial nature and reduce aggression.

Dwarf puffer fish are not known for being prolific jumpers, but it may happen, especially if they are stressed or scared or tank conditions are unsuitable. To minimise the risk: use a tight-fitting lid, lower the water level, use floating plants, etc.

These fish do not tolerate ammonia, nitrites or nitrates well. It is absolutely crucial to ensure the cycling process is complete before adding them to the aquarium. Ideally, wait at least a couple of weeks until the balance is completely established.

Monitor the water parameters regularly and do water changes every week.

Decorations and plants: Dwarf puffer fish require plenty of hiding places, such as driftwood, plants, leaves, pipes, etc. Decorations allow them to establish territories and create visual barriers, helping to reduce conflicts, and give them places to retreat when stressed or threatened.

A study examined the survival of Carinotetraodon travancoricus with Cabomba and Ceratophyllum. Cabomba worked better than Ceratophyllum, and planting Cabomba 5–7.5 cm (2–3 inches) apart led to higher survival rates.

Placing these fish in open aquariums is a huge mistake; the open layout is unsettling for them.

• Temperature: 24–27°C (75–80°F). They do not tolerate cooler temperatures well.
  • pH: 7.0–8.0. In their natural environment they thrive in alkaline waters; reducing the pH to 6.5 had negative effects on the fish.
  • Hardness: 7–14 GH. They do not like soft water.

• Lighting: dim lighting is optimal; bright light stresses them.
  • Water flow: still or very slow currents are recommended.
  • Substrate: mud and sand in the natural environment.
  • Filtration: no special requirements, as long as the filter suits the size of the tank.

Studies go against the common idea that this fish is exclusively carnivorous. One gut content analysis suggested it is an omnivore: insects (18.52%), crustaceans (18.07%), annelids (14.30%), diatoms (14.02%), green algae (12.55%), sand (10.78%) and detritus (11.77%). Another study found that algae constituted more than 60% of both male and female diets, along with red worms and semi-digested animal matter, mainly crustaceans and insect parts.

In the aquarium, they can be fed a wide variety of live food:

  • brine shrimp (Artemia salina)
  • Artemia nauplii
  • daphnia
  • fruit flies
  • moina
  • vinegar eels
  • mosquito larvae
  • cyclops
  • detritus worms
  • bloodworms
  • blackworms
  • tubifex worms
  • small live snails, etc.

Feeding tips:

  • Feeding is the most challenging aspect of care; they are pretty picky eaters.
  • They may refuse frozen foods such as shrimp or clams.
  • They rarely eat flakes, pellets or other dry food; try combining with live food.
  • They are not fast swimmers, so in a community aquarium they are often outcompeted for food.
  • Nothing triggers their appetite more than live, moving prey.
  • They may pick at algae and detritus from time to time, but the diet should still consist primarily of meaty foods.
  • Feeding twice a day (morning and evening) significantly reduces tail-nipping of tankmates.

Plants: They are completely safe in planted tanks and do not eat living plant material.

Sociality: In the wild, Dwarf puffer fish are not very social and do not swim in large groups, although a pair tends to stay about 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches) apart.

Temper: They are quite territorial and aggressive, especially towards their own kind and during mating. Males are far more aggressive and should not be kept in small tanks. Monitor behaviour and be prepared to separate individuals if aggression becomes excessive. They may also show aggression to other fish, even bigger ones, and nip at slow-moving or long-finned species, so tankmates must be chosen carefully. A heavily planted tank is highly recommended to establish territories and minimise aggression. Breaking the line of sight with decorations, plants or other features is an effective strategy.

Activity: Active and curious, they explore their surroundings with a jerky, hovering motion like mini helicopters, which lets them navigate precisely through plants and decorations. They are not particularly fast swimmers. Like other pufferfish, they can inflate their abdomen when threatened; if a larger predator tries to eat it, both fish can end up dying.

Placement in tank: They prefer to hang out near the bottom and swim in the middle of the tank, particularly in areas with dense vegetation or hiding places.

  • Social level: yes, but can be kept alone
  • Activity: medium
  • Placement: middle and bottom dwellers
  • Peaceful: semi-aggressive
  • Territorial: yes
  • Nippers: yes

Tankmates: Keeping them with others is a significant challenge. Stories of peaceful coexistence exist, but in most cases it is only a matter of time; the best choice is a species-only aquarium.

If kept in a community tank anyway (not recommended), tankmates should be small fish that are not big enough to eat or harass them, such as Neon Tetras, Harlequin Rasboras, Clown Killifish, Least Killifish, Otocinclus, Danio rerio, Pygmy Cory and Kuhli loach.

Dwarf shrimp: Do not keep with dwarf shrimp. These predators will eat shrimplets, and even adult shrimp after molting may be eaten. They can go after prey much larger than themselves, including Amano shrimp and Ghost shrimp. Heavily planted tanks give some protection, but it is a bad idea in the long run.

Snails: Not compatible with any freshwater snail. They kill snails, mostly smaller ones, but eat only what protrudes from the shell. The rest of the meat remains and can raise nitrogen levels as it decays.

Avoid:

  • Larger or aggressive fish
  • Dwarf shrimp
  • Most crayfish and freshwater crab species
  • Even dwarf frogs

This species has clear sexual dimorphism and differential colour patterns, though these are not easily recognised in juveniles.

  • Females may have a more rounded body than males, especially when carrying eggs.
  • The coloration of males, especially during the breeding season, is much more vivid.

Males have a dark bluish band extending from the mouth to the caudal fin on the ventral side, with a clear dark line running medially on the ventral surface. Males also have a distinct pattern of closely arranged wrinkles just behind the eyes. The abdominal region of males is yellow, with golden orange at the base of the caudal, anal and dorsal fins, in addition to a dark line on the caudal fin. Females have light black spots throughout the body, which mark the shining golden yellow spots.

Breeding can be a bit challenging, but it is possible even in home aquariums.

Maturity: Females mature slightly earlier than males. First sexual maturity is at 18.33 mm (0.72 inches) in males and 18.0 mm (0.71 inches) in females.

Spawning: Males attract females to the spawning site by swimming back and forth between the site and the females, often directing them by pushing them with the body and nibbling the belly. A female ready to spawn follows the leading male. They do not eat much during spawning.

Fecundity: Typically up to 10 eggs at a time, with up to 10 or more spawning bouts per spawning sequence. According to research, absolute fecundity ranges from 139 to 480.

Eggs: They are egg scatterers, not livebearers. The female releases eggs and the male fertilises them in the water; the eggs fall and adhere to surfaces such as plants or substrate. Eggs are about 1.43 mm in diameter, spherical, demersal and adhesive, with a mass of small oil globules.

Parental care: None, except defence of the spawning territory by males.

Incubation: Eggs hatch after 7 days at 22–24°C (71–75°F) and 5 days at 26–28°C (79–84°F).

Fry: Hatched fry are about 3.5 mm long with incomplete eye development. They have brownish bodies and two translucent vertical bands, one behind a large yolk sac and one at the end of the caudal fin. They can attach to surfaces using the underside of the yolk sac. The yolk is typically consumed after 4 days, and they start free-swimming after 6 days.

  • 20 days after hatching: about 6.26 mm (0.25 inches)
  • 62 days: about 10.18 mm (0.4 inches)
  • 112 days: about 14.75 mm (0.58 inches)
  • 180 days: mean size about 16.6 mm (0.6 inches)

Feeding fry: Once the yolk is depleted, fry need rotifers, microworms and Artemia for the first 2 weeks.

Separate breeding tank: Other fish, conspecifics or even snails can eat the newly laid eggs, so a separate breeding tank is recommended to increase egg and fry survival. It should have fine-leaved plants or spawning mops where the eggs can be scattered and protected from adult pufferfish, with stable and suitable water conditions (temperature, pH and hardness) that mimic the natural habitat.

Description

Adults are 2.5 to 3 cm (1 to 1.2 inches) long, though most are 2–2.5 cm (0.8–1 inch).

  • Body shape: ovoid in general, except the caudal area; covered with soft spines in both sexes; the tail base is short and thick.
  • Coloration: yellowish dorsally and whitish below; the dorsal side is brownish to green with irregular spots.
  • Patterns: two black oval patches on the sides before the dorsal fin, a dark wide stripe from the top to the bottom fins on the sides, two irregular dark patches and a V-shaped mark behind the eyes, a narrow light stripe around the eyes, and irregular bands and triangular patches on the back. All fin rays are yellowish.
  • Fins: rounded; dorsal fin 7–8 rays, anal fin 8 rays, pectoral fin 16–17 rays; ventral fin absent.
  • Eyes: very large "puppy" eyes; the lower margin of the eye is slightly below the mouth corner.
  • Head and mouth: large, blunt head; the jaw forms a beak of four heavy, powerful teeth, two above and two below.

Lifespan

In the wild, lifespan is estimated at about 4 years. In aquariums with appropriate conditions they can live 6–8 years, with reports of even longer.

Taxonomy and etymology

In 1941, Indian ichthyologists S.L. Hora and K.K. Nair first described this fish as Tetraodon travancoricus. In 1975, W. J. Dekkers reviewed the genus Tetraodon and considered Carinotetraodon a synonym of Tetraodon. In 1999, Ralf Britz and Maurice Kottelat showed that this fish has the modified parapophyses of Carinotetraodon and transferred it to that genus. The genus currently comprises 6 valid species of dwarf pufferfishes restricted to freshwaters in Asia.

The genus name is derived from the Latin "Carino" (keel or ridge) and the Greek "Tetraodon" (four teeth). The species name comes from the region of Travancore in Kerala, India.
